Yes. The strongest direct match is a graph-based reaction foundation model: RxnCLF represents each reaction as a condensed reaction graph that merges reactants and products, then uses self-supervised contrastive learning to learn transformation-aware reaction embeddings for reactivity and yield prediction [1]. It outperforms graph- and sequence-based baselines on multiple yield prediction benchmarks and is intended to support other reaction informatics tasks such as regioselectivity, enantioselectivity, and condition optimization [1].

Other graph machine learning work is adjacent but differs in focus. enviGraph uses graph-to-sequence pretraining for biodegradation product and pathway prediction, improving some benchmark results with synthetic reaction pretraining [6]. ReACT-Drug applies reinforcement learning over chemically valid, reaction-template-based transformations for de novo drug design rather than reaction prediction itself [4]. The remaining papers are mainly language-model or general molecular graph methods rather than graph ML specifically for chemical reactions [2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10].
